title: Feature Stores
description: Understand online vs offline feature serving, training-serving skew, Feast architecture, feature freshness guarantees, and Uber's Michelangelo platform.

segments.text: ML models are only as good as their features. But computing features consistently across training and serving is hard. During training, you compute features from historical data. During serving, you compute them in real-time. If these computations differ even slightly — a different aggregation window or a missing normalization — your model's accuracy degrades silently. This is training-serving skew.

Feature stores separate into online and offline layers. Offline store: historical features in a data warehouse for training — batch-computed, potentially terabytes. Online store: latest feature values in Redis or DynamoDB for real-time inference — sub-millisecond latency, gigabytes. Both must produce identical feature values to prevent skew.

Feast is the leading open-source feature store. Data scientists define features in Python, Feast materializes them from batch sources to the online store. Feature definitions are version-controlled. A serving API returns features by entity key in sub-ten-milliseconds. Feast supports BigQuery, Snowflake, and Redshift as offline sources, and Redis and DynamoDB as online stores.

Feature freshness guarantees define how current your features are. Batch features might be one day stale — user's lifetime purchase count. Stream features should be minutes fresh — user's transaction count in the last hour. Real-time features are computed at request time — current session duration. Each freshness level has different infrastructure costs and complexity.

Your fraud detection model uses a feature 'number of transactions in the last hour.' During training, this is computed from historical data in batch. During serving, it must be computed in real-time. How do you ensure both produce identical results?
segments.thought_prompt: How do you guarantee that batch-computed and real-time-computed versions of the same feature produce identical results?

segments.text: Uber's Michelangelo is an end-to-end ML platform. Its feature store computes features from Kafka streams and Hive tables. Features are stored with metadata — owner, description, data type, freshness SLA. Any team can discover and reuse features. Before Michelangelo, Uber had one hundred teams computing the same features independently with inconsistent results.

Feature engineering at scale means computing features across billions of entities. Point-in-time correctness is critical — when computing features for a training example from January 15th, you must use only data available before January 15th. Using future data creates data leakage and inflates model metrics. This temporal join is the hardest part of feature store implementation.

Feature monitoring catches data quality issues before they affect model predictions. Monitor feature distributions — drift detection using KL divergence or PSI. Alert on null rate changes, value range violations, and staleness. A feature that was ninety-nine percent non-null suddenly becoming fifty percent null indicates a pipeline failure upstream.

Feature reuse across teams provides compound value. If the risk team computes a 'user trust score' feature, the recommendations team can reuse it without reimplementing. Feature stores enable this through a catalog with search, lineage tracking, and access controls. LinkedIn's feature store serves features to over one hundred ML models from a shared catalog.

Design a feature store for a company with fifty ML models, three thousand features, real-time and batch feature requirements, and a team of one hundred data scientists. What are your architecture and governance decisions?

segments.text: Feature stores solve training-serving skew by providing a single source of truth for features. Online stores serve real-time inference, offline stores serve training. Point-in-time correctness prevents data leakage. Feature monitoring catches drift. And shared catalogs enable cross-team reuse. The Staff-level insight: the feature store is as critical as the model itself — garbage features mean garbage predictions.
